setup.name: Department of Buildings alteration filing fee
setup.note: NYC Admin. Code §28-112.2 fee table (also in Local Law 77 of 2023, nyc.gov): alterations in buildings other than 1-3 family homes, under 7 stories and 100,000 sq ft: Alteration Type 2 minimum filing fee $225 for the first $3,000 of cost plus $10.30 for each additional $1,000 (Type 1: $280; Type 3 and Limited Alteration Application: $195). $70,000 light renovation: 225 + 67 x 10.30 = $915; $180,000: $2,048; $320,000: $3,490. waitDays: NYS Comptroller audit (July 2026): in 2025 DOB took 20.3 days on average from application to approval, 23.6 days in the first four months of FY2026; first plan review alone 3.7 business days. The engine should compute the fee from the build-out cost of the address.

setup.name: Asbestos investigation (ACP-5) before the permit
setup.agency: NYC Department of Environmental Protection (certified asbestos investigator)
setup.note: Rule seen in the DOB page extract: an ACP-5 (not an asbestos project) or other asbestos form must be submitted before a DOB permit may be issued; work in buildings built after April 1, 1987 may use the ASB4 exemption. Only a DEP-certified asbestos investigator can file it. Price is my estimate: secondary guides quote $400-$1,500 for an NYC ACP-5 survey plus $25-$150 per lab sample; $900 is the midpoint for a small storefront with a handful of samples. No official price exists. The 7 days are my estimate for scheduling, sampling and lab results.

setup.name: Landmarks permit for storefront work (historic districts only)
setup.appliesIf: address is in a historic district or the building is a landmark
setup.note: LPC storefront fact sheet (2019) seen in extract: a complete storefront application gets a staff permit within 10 business days through FasTrack, otherwise within 15 business days (about 21 calendar days); incomplete applications are returned. LPC said in April 2025 that 95% of its approvals are issued at staff level. Any exterior storefront change in a historic district (sign, awning, door, window) needs the permit, and DOB will not issue its permit without it. Proposals that go to the full Commission take months (one architect guide: 90 business days or more). Fee, LPC fees page seen in extract: a flat $95 for the first $25,000 of work plus $5 for each $1,000 above, collected through the DOB NOW filing; for a $70,000 job 95 + 45 x 5 = $320.

setup.name: Letter of No Objection for an old building without a Certificate of Occupancy
setup.agency: NYC Department of Buildings, borough office
setup.appliesIf: building built or altered before 1938 with no Certificate of Occupancy on file
setup.note: DOB page seen in extract: for buildings built or altered before 1938, when no Certificate of Occupancy was required, a Letter of No Objection confirms the legal use. For a cafe it has to say "eating and drinking establishment". Wait: one architecture firm says at least one month in a clear case; requests can be denied until related applications are signed off. The DOB fee for the letter was not found in this session, so cost is 0 plus the expediter time already inside architect_expediter.

setup.name: Build-out contingency reserve
setup.note: 15% of a $70,000 light renovation. NYC contractors recommend a contingency of 10-15% of hard costs (another Brooklyn contractor says 5-10% is typical); change orders rushed through without a reserve carry a 15-30% premium. The research notes budget $9,500 for the same scenario. This is a reserve, not a purchase: money not eaten by the events of extra.eventCatalog (hidden conditions, change orders, failed inspections) stays in the bank.

setup.name: Sales tax on the contractor's bill (if the work is not a capital improvement)
setup.avoidableBy: lease clause that makes the improvements the landlord's property on installation, plus Form ST-124 given to the contractor
setup.note: NYS Tax Department advisory opinion TSB-A-24(54)S and the Capital Improvements bulletin, seen in extract: installations made by or for a tenant are presumed temporary, so they are not capital improvements unless the lease shows permanence; without a properly completed Form ST-124 the contractor must collect tax on the charges. Materials are taxed either way. Calculation: 8.875% on the labor-and-markup share of the bill (my assumption: 60%) x $70,000 = $3,728; on the full $70,000 the tax would be $6,212.

setup.name: Con Edison security deposit for a new business account
setup.note: Con Edison's rights document for non-residential customers, seen in extract: the deposit may not be more than two times the average monthly bill for the previous calendar year (two times peak-season usage for seasonal businesses), and the customer may ask for a review. For a new shop the utility estimates from a similar business. Calculation: electricity taken as $800 of the pack's $1,100 utilities line x 2 = $1,600. Already counted inside the existing insurance_utility_deposits item ($1,500): do not charge both.

setup.name: Electrical service upgrade for espresso, ice and refrigeration loads
setup.appliesIf: space class is standard or heavy, or the panel cannot carry the equipment load
setup.note: Weak estimate, quote-only in real life. NYC electricians advertise $3,500-$10,000 for a 100 to 200 amp panel upgrade in a home; a commercial three-phase service costs more, so the top of that range is used. Any service change needs Con Edison coordination, which adds two to six weeks (contractor guides); Con Edison's own 2021 sheet for fleet chargers says utility-side upgrades can run 6 to 24 months depending on the existing service and the requested load. Con Edison's guide describes the path: a licensed contractor files the request, the utility issues a service layout, then inspections.

setup.name: Health Department consultative inspection (optional, ungraded)
setup.agency: NYC Department of Health and Mental Hygiene (DOHMH)
setup.note: NYC Health Code Chapter 21 and NYC311, seen in extract: an applicant for a new permit may request a consultative inspection before the first graded inspection for $100 (only after the shop has begun serving food); for an existing establishment between cycles the fee is $400. The inspector issues no violations and no points, but a public health hazard must be fixed before the inspector leaves or the shop can be closed. Game use: paying it lowers the points found at the first graded inspection.

setup.name: Sales tax on the furniture and equipment bought with a business
setup.note: NYS Tax Bulletin TB-ST-70 (Bulk Sales), seen in extract: the purchaser owes sales tax on the tangible personal property bought in a bulk sale (furniture, fixtures, supplies), except inventory for resale; the tax is paid to the seller with the seller's final return or directly to the Tax Department. Calculation: 8.875% x $40,000 of the price allocated to furniture, fixtures and equipment (my allocation for a small cafe; goodwill and the lease are not taxed) = $3,550.

setup.name: Franchise fee (example: Gregorys Coffee)
setup.agency: Franchisor; the offering must be registered with the NYS Attorney General
setup.note: Gregorys Coffee franchise site, seen in extract: initial franchise fee $35,000, training fee $0-$3,000, royalty 6% of gross sales; a franchise directory adds a 2.5% marketing fund and a total initial investment of $459,150-$946,000 from the disclosure document (another summary: $424,000-$903,000); the brand asks for $200,000 in liquid assets and $500,000 net worth. Franchising launched in early 2026 with Craveworthy Brands (Daily Coffee News, Feb 18, 2026). Dunkin' for comparison: franchise fee $40,000-$90,000, royalty 5.9%, advertising 5%, total $443,000-$1,832,500 (Inspire Brands site, disclosure document of March 26, 2026).

setup.name: Franchise training fee and pre-opening travel
setup.note: Gregorys Coffee franchise site, seen in extract: initial training fee $0 to $3,000; the top of the range is used. Travel and wages during training are on the franchisee.

setup.name: Mobile Food Vending License (the vendor's personal license)
setup.agency: NYC Department of Health and Mental Hygiene (DOHMH)
setup.note: NYC Business and NYC311 (KA-01830), seen in extract: the two-year license costs $50; veterans are exempt. The Mobile Food Vendor Food Protection Course is a separate $53. It is needed before applying for a unit permit, and only current license holders may join the waiting lists for supervisory licenses. The 30 days are my estimate for the food protection course for mobile vendors, the application and the ID card; no official processing time was seen.

setup.name: Mobile Food Vending Unit permit (the cart's decal)
setup.agency: NYC Department of Health and Mental Hygiene (DOHMH)
setup.note: NYC Business and Health Code Chapter 6, seen in extract: the two-year full-term permit costs $75 for a non-processing unit and $200 for a processing unit (seasonal: $15 and $35); veterans pay nothing. A coffee cart is Class D, a non-processing unit serving foods that need no temperature control "such as brewed coffee and tea", so $75 applies; add milk-based drinks that need refrigeration and the class, the cart and the fee change. Two weeks after applying you call for a pre-permit inspection and must pass it within six months, in person, with a commissary agreement in hand: the 180 days are that outer limit. The real gate is the cap: a year-round permit now requires a supervisory license, and Local Laws 54 and 59 of 2026 add 2,200 of those a year from fiscal 2027 to 2031 (311 KA-03354) against a waiting list that advocates put above 20,000.

setup.name: Coffee cart built to Health Department specifications
setup.note: One current listing for a full-service stainless coffee cart: $16,500. For scale: a New York-built stainless hot dog cart starts at $5,790 (800 Buy Cart, Model 201), and licensed used carts resell for $8,000-$25,000 according to one vendor guide. No price list for a cart pre-approved by the Health Department was found. Lifespan is my estimate.

setup.name: Temporary Food Service Establishment permit (markets, street fairs, pop-ups)
setup.agency: NYC Department of Health and Mental Hygiene (DOHMH)
setup.note: NYC311 and NYC Business, seen in extract: the permit costs $70 a year (plus $25 if you make frozen desserts), covers events that last 14 days or less, and one permit serves one event at a time: a second simultaneous event needs a second permit. Event organizers must notify the Health Department 30 days before the event with the list of vendors and their permit numbers; that notice period is used as the wait. A vendor without a valid permit faces a summons of $200-$2,000 and immediate closing of the stand.

officials.name: Buildings inspector
officials.realProcess: Most visits start with a 311 complaint from a neighbor or a competitor about noise, dust or a dumpster. The inspector checks the posted permits against the work in progress. Work with no permit gets a violation and a Stop Work Order; the order is lifted only after the permit is obtained and the civil penalties are paid.

officials.name: Street vending enforcement officer
officials.agency: NYC Department of Sanitation, Office of Vending Enforcement, with NYPD and DOHMH
officials.realProcess: Officers walk vending corridors and answer 311 complaints from storefront businesses. They ask for the vendor's license and check the permit decal on the cart. A vendor with neither gets a summons returnable to the city's hearings office, and a cart with no licensed person at it can be seized.

violations.name: Construction work without a Department of Buildings permit
violations.law: NYC Admin. Code §28-105.1 (permit required), §28-213.1 (civil penalty for work without a permit), §28-207.2 (stop work orders)
violations.fineFormula: 21 x the permit fee, minimum $6,000, maximum $15,000 (buildings other than 1-2 family homes); the permit must still be obtained
violations.criminal: Knowingly continuing work without a permit or against a Stop Work Order can be prosecuted as a misdemeanor under Title 28.
violations.note: DOB service notices on Local Law 156 of 2017, seen in extract: the civil penalty for work without a permit on buildings other than one- or two-family homes is 21 times the permit fee, minimum $6,000, maximum $15,000 (homes: 6 times, $600-$10,000). An older rule text (1 RCNY 102-04: 14 times or $5,000) still circulates; the 2017 law superseded it. With the $915 fee of a $70,000 job, 21 x 915 = $19,215, capped at $15,000; the base here is the legal minimum. On top comes a separate hearing-office violation, and the permit, drawings and fees still have to be paid for. closureDays is not a legal figure: it is my estimate of the standstill while plans are drawn, filed and approved under a Stop Work Order (application-to-approval averaged 20.3 days in 2025, plus drawings).

violations.name: Working against a Stop Work Order
violations.law: NYC Admin. Code §28-207.2.2 and §28-207.2.6 (civil penalties for violating a stop work order)
violations.fineFormula: $6,000 for the first offense, $12,000 for each subsequent offense; the order is not rescinded until the penalty is paid
violations.criminal: Violating a Stop Work Order is a misdemeanor; DOB publishes offenders in its monthly enforcement bulletin.
violations.note: DOB Stop Work Order page, seen in extract: "First Offense - $6,000; Subsequent Offenses - $12,000"; the Department will not rescind a Stop Work Order until these civil penalties have been paid; work that fixes an unsafe condition is exempt. DOB enforcement bulletins show much larger totals when unpermitted work continues against an order (one 2020s case: $188,750 for one site). closureDays is my estimate of the extra standstill.

violations.name: Plumbing or electrical work by an unlicensed person
violations.law: NYC Admin. Code §28-408.1 (plumbing only by a licensed master plumber), §28-410.1, §27-3017 (electrical work only by a licensed electrician); Local Law 46 of 2017
violations.criminal: Unlicensed plumbing or electrical work is a misdemeanor under Title 28; the work has to be opened up, redone by a licensed firm and inspected.
violations.note: Local Law 46 of 2017 (nyc.gov) sets minimum civil penalties for unlicensed plumbing and fire suppression work; the figures were cut off in the extract. The base is one reported hearing-office case (CityLand, 2022): a plumber working with no licensed master plumber supervising was fined $5,000. The real cost is larger: the utility and DOB will not sign off work that no licensed firm filed, so it is redone. closureDays is my estimate for the redo and re-inspection.

violations.name: Vending food from a cart with no license or no unit permit
violations.law: NYC Admin. Code §17-307(a)(1) (license) and §17-307(b) (unit permit); forfeiture under §17-321 and §17-322
violations.criminal: Unlicensed vending has also been charged as a misdemeanor; a 2025-2026 Council bill to repeal the criminal penalties was pending when checked. A cart with no licensed vendor at it can be seized and forfeited.
violations.note: Health Department penalty schedule and the city's vending enforcement page, seen in extract: unlicensed mobile food vendor in a public space $1,000; a unit with no permit $1,000; "fines start at $1,000 for mobile food vendors". Seizure and forfeiture of the cart come from Admin. Code §17-321/322 (court decision seen in extract). closureDays is my estimate for getting a seized cart back or replacing it.

violations.name: Selling food at a market or pop-up without a temporary permit
violations.law: NYC Health Code §88.05 and Article 5 (permit required for a temporary food service establishment)
violations.note: NYC Health page on food vending at temporary events, seen in extract: vendors without a valid permit can receive a summons subject to fines of $200 to $2,000 and the stand can be closed immediately. The base is the bottom of that range; closureDays 1 = the event day lost. The Health Code section number is from my reading of Article 88 and should be checked against the code text.

violations.name: Bought a business without notifying the Tax Department (bulk sale)
violations.law: NY Tax Law §1141(c); 20 NYCRR Part 537; Form AU-196.10
violations.fineFormula: the seller's unpaid sales tax, penalty and interest, up to the purchase price or the fair market value of the assets, whichever is higher; not a fine but an inherited debt
violations.note: NYS Tax Bulletin TB-ST-70 and Form AU-196.10, seen in extract: the purchaser must file Form AU-196.10 at least 10 days before paying for or taking possession of the assets; within 5 business days the Department answers with a release (AU-197.1) or a Notice of Claim (AU-196.2), and within 90 days states the amount; a purchaser who does not file, or files late, is personally liable for the seller's sales tax up to the higher of the purchase price or fair market value, whether or not money was withheld from the seller. Division of Tax Appeals cases against delis and restaurants show the Department using this (Bernard & Varecha Deli, 1646 Kosher Deli). Game reading: "saved" is the seller's hidden sales-tax debt carried by the listing, so pctOfSaved 1 means the buyer pays that debt in full. The debt per listing is a design value, not a statistic.

shortcuts.name: Renovate without filing plans
shortcuts.what: Skip the architect, the asbestos report and the Buildings permit and start demolition next week. You save the fees and about a month. One 311 call brings an inspector: Stop Work Order, a penalty of at least $6,000, and you still have to file.
shortcuts.savesNote: architect_expediter $7,000 + dob_alteration_filing_fee $915 + asbestos_survey_acp5 $900 = $8,815, plus about 30 days of rent ($6,000) not counted here

shortcuts.name: Keep the crew working under a Stop Work Order
shortcuts.what: The inspector taped a Stop Work Order to the door, but every idle week is $1,400 of rent. Work at night and hope nobody calls. If caught: $6,000, then $12,000 each time after, and the order stays until you pay.
shortcuts.savesNote: two weeks of rent that would otherwise be paid on an idle site = half a month of rent

shortcuts.name: Let a handyman do the plumbing and wiring
shortcuts.what: A licensed plumber and electrician quote twice what the handyman does. Unlicensed work cannot be filed or inspected: if anyone looks, it is torn out and redone by a licensed firm, with a fine on top.
shortcuts.savesNote: my estimate: licensed plumbing and electrical hookups are about $12,000 of a $70,000 light renovation; a handyman halves that

shortcuts.name: Keep trading on the seller's Health permit
shortcuts.what: You bought the shop on Friday and want to sell coffee on Monday. The seller's permit died with the sale: permits cannot be transferred. Until yours is issued, or 22 days after you applied, you are running a restaurant with no permit.
shortcuts.savesNote: three weeks of sales kept in the takeover month, net of cost of goods: roughly half a month of revenue; applies once

shortcuts.name: Close the purchase without the bulk-sale notice
shortcuts.what: The seller wants the money this week and the notice to the Tax Department adds at least 10 days, maybe 90. Skip it and every dollar of sales tax the seller never paid becomes your personal debt, up to the price you paid.
shortcuts.savesNote: my estimate: ten days of rent on a shop you cannot yet take over ($2,000 at $6,000 a month); the legal fee for the filing is small

shortcuts.name: Roll the cart out without a permit
shortcuts.what: The waiting list for a cart permit is years long. Vend anyway and each stop by an enforcement officer costs $1,000 or more; a cart with no licensed vendor can be seized.
shortcuts.savesNote: the alternative to waiting is renting someone else's permit, reported at $20,000-$25,000 for two years, about $833-$1,040 a month (secondary sources); renting is itself illegal because permits are not transferable

shortcuts.name: Run a pop-up stand with no temporary permit
shortcuts.what: The market is this weekend and the paperwork wants 30 days of notice. Set up anyway: if an inspector walks the market, the stand is closed on the spot and the summons runs $200 to $2,000.
shortcuts.savesNote: the $70 permit fee; the real gain is the weekend's sales

reports.name: Report construction without a permit (311)
reports.text: The Department of Buildings sends an inspector to check the posted permits against the work. If there is no permit, the site is stopped and fined. If the work is legal, you get a warning for a false complaint.

reports.name: Report an unlicensed food cart or stand (311)
reports.text: Vending enforcement checks the vendor's license and the cart's permit decal. No license or no permit means a $1,000 summons and possibly a seized cart. If the papers are in order, you get a warning.

roadmap.title: Choose how you enter: build, buy, franchise, cart or pop-up
roadmap.text: Building in a former cafe costs the least cash but takes 5-9 months before the first sale. Buying an operating shop costs about 2 times its yearly owner earnings and sells coffee from week four. A franchise needs $400,000 or more. A cart or a market stand starts under $25,000 but depends on a capped permit.

roadmap.title: Look up the address before you fall in love with it
roadmap.text: Search the building in the Department of Buildings records: Certificate of Occupancy, open violations, Stop Work Orders, landmark status. A building with open violations can hold up your permit, and work on a landmark needs a second approval.

roadmap.title: Walk the space with an architect and an electrician
roadmap.text: Check the electrical panel against your equipment load, the water line, the drain and grease interceptor, ventilation, the bathroom and the step at the door. An undersized panel means weeks of Con Edison coordination; a missing drain means a heavy conversion at $400 per sq ft instead of $90.

roadmap.title: Decide on gas before you sign: check availability or go all-electric
roadmap.text: A 2017 State Senate survey found restaurants waited 68 days on average for gas service, some up to a year. Con Edison answers a gas-availability request for a food business before you sign. A coffee shop with no cooking can run all-electric and skip the wait.
roadmap.agency: Con Edison (Manhattan, Bronx, part of Queens) or National Grid (Brooklyn, Staten Island, part of Queens)

roadmap.title: Fix the deal in a letter of intent
roadmap.text: Before lawyers draft 60-100 pages, agree in writing on rent, term, free rent, yearly increases (3% is typical), the deposit, the guaranty, what the landlord delivers, and that rent starts only after permits. The landlord usually pays the broker.

roadmap.title: Get the lease reviewed, free if you qualify
roadmap.text: The city's Commercial Lease Assistance Program gives eligible small businesses a free lawyer to review and negotiate a lease before signing; a provider calls back within three business days. It does not go to court for you. Otherwise budget $3,500 for your own lawyer.
roadmap.agency: NYC Department of Small Business Services

roadmap.title: Negotiate the personal guaranty
roadmap.text: A full guaranty makes you personally owe every remaining month of a 10-year lease. A good guy guaranty ends your liability once you give written notice (usually 3-6 months), pay rent to the day you leave and hand back the keys broom-clean. Landlords trade it for a larger deposit.

roadmap.title: Negotiate free rent and the rent start date
roadmap.text: NYC restaurant leases typically give 3-6 months of free rent for the build-out, up to 12 for a heavy job on a 10-year lease. Tie the rent start to permits, not to a calendar date: if approvals slip, the free months run out while the room is still a construction site.

roadmap.title: Add the clause that saves sales tax on the build-out
roadmap.text: New York presumes a tenant's installations are temporary and taxes the contractor's bill at 8.875%. If the lease says improvements become the landlord's property when installed, the work can qualify as a capital improvement: give the contractor Form ST-124 and the labor is not taxed.
roadmap.agency: NYS Department of Taxation and Finance

roadmap.title: Ask the city for a free project manager
roadmap.text: Since the July 2026 executive order, the NYC Business Express Service Team assigns each new business a project manager who lists the permits you need, helps file them and coordinates the pre-opening inspections across agencies. It costs nothing.
roadmap.agency: NYC Department of Small Business Services (NYC BEST)

roadmap.title: File the alteration with the Department of Buildings
roadmap.text: A registered architect or engineer files the plans in DOB NOW. The fee is $225 for the first $3,000 of work plus $10.30 per $1,000 after: $915 on a $70,000 job. Approval averaged 20 days in 2025. Painting, flooring and new cabinets alone need no permit.

roadmap.title: Order the asbestos investigation
roadmap.text: In a building from before April 1987 the Buildings permit is not issued until a certified asbestos investigator files an ACP-5 report. If the old floor tile or pipe wrap tests positive, licensed abatement comes first and the schedule slips by weeks.

roadmap.title: In a historic district: get the Landmarks permit first
roadmap.text: Any change to a storefront in a historic district (sign, awning, door, glass) needs a Landmarks permit before the Buildings permit. Complete applications are approved by staff in 10-15 business days; the fee is $95 for the first $25,000 of work plus $5 per $1,000.

roadmap.title: Old building with no Certificate of Occupancy: get a Letter of No Objection
roadmap.text: Buildings from before 1938 often have no Certificate of Occupancy. The Buildings borough office can issue a Letter of No Objection saying an eating and drinking establishment is a legal use. Allow at least a month, and make the lease conditional on getting it.

roadmap.title: Take three bids and sign a contract with a payment schedule
roadmap.text: Plumbing and wiring must be done by licensed firms. Ask for insurance certificates naming you and the landlord: under New York's scaffold law the tenant who hires the crew can be liable for a worker's fall. Pay by milestones and collect lien waivers; hold 10-15% in reserve.

roadmap.title: Order long-lead equipment before the walls close
roadmap.text: Order the espresso machine, the refrigeration and any custom counter as soon as the plans are approved. Imported machines have carried a 15% US tariff on EU goods since mid-2025, and the plumber and electrician need the exact models to rough in the lines.

roadmap.title: Open the Con Edison account and file any service request early
roadmap.text: A new business account can require a deposit of up to twice the average monthly bill. If the panel must grow, your licensed electrician files the request and Con Edison issues a service layout: allow two to six weeks, far longer if the street side needs work.

roadmap.title: Pass the trade inspections and close out the permit
roadmap.text: Plumbing and electrical work is inspected before the walls are closed, then the job is signed off. The Health Department's pre-permit inspection needs all construction finished and no food on site. Open permits left behind become your problem at sale or renewal.
roadmap.agency: NYC Department of Buildings; NYC DOHMH

roadmap.title: Soft-open, then book the $100 consultative inspection
roadmap.text: Once you have begun serving food and before your first graded inspection, the Health Department will send an inspector for $100 who points out problems and issues no violations. Fix what they find before the unannounced graded visit decides the letter in your window.

roadmap.title: Buying a shop: read the listing like a lender
roadmap.text: US coffee shops sold in 2021-2025 went for a median 0.41 times yearly sales and 2.0 times owner earnings. New York asking prices run 1.6 to 3.1 times stated cash flow. "Key money" listings sell a built-out room and a lease, not customers.

roadmap.title: Buying a shop: prove the sales and find the liens
roadmap.text: Match 24 months of register reports to bank deposits and to the sales tax returns the seller filed. "We do more in cash than the books show" is unprovable and not worth paying for. Check that the espresso machine is owned, not leased or pledged to a lender.

roadmap.title: Buying a shop: get the landlord's consent in writing
roadmap.text: The lease decides whether the deal exists. Most leases need the landlord's consent to an assignment; some let the landlord take the space back instead. Expect a new deposit and your own guaranty. Check the years left: a shop that loses its lease rarely survives a move.

roadmap.title: Buying a shop: notify the Tax Department 10 days before you pay
roadmap.text: File Form AU-196.10 at least 10 days before paying or taking possession. The state answers within 5 business days: a release, or a claim that freezes the money in escrow for up to 90 days. Skip it and the seller's unpaid sales tax is yours, up to the price.
roadmap.agency: NYS Department of Taxation and Finance

roadmap.title: Buying a shop: apply for every permit in your own name
roadmap.text: The Health permit is void the moment the business changes hands. Apply at least 22 days before closing so you can trade from day one, and register for sales tax 20 days ahead. New insurance, a new Con Edison account. The seller's unemployment-insurance rate follows you.
roadmap.agency: NYC DOHMH; NYS Tax Department; NYS Department of Labor

roadmap.title: Buying a shop: close, pay the tax on the equipment, keep the regulars
roadmap.text: At closing you owe 8.875% sales tax on the furniture and equipment part of the price. Keep the staff the regulars know, keep the recipes for a month, and write a training period and a non-compete for the seller into the contract.

roadmap.title: Franchise: read the disclosure document and call franchisees
roadmap.text: A franchisor must give you its disclosure document at least 14 calendar days before you sign or pay, and must be registered with the New York Attorney General. Item 7 shows the full investment, Item 6 the royalties, Item 20 how many units closed. Call owners on the list.
roadmap.agency: Federal Trade Commission; NYS Attorney General

roadmap.title: Franchise: site approval, mandated build-out, training
roadmap.text: The franchisor approves the address and dictates the design, equipment and suppliers, so the build-out is not yours to trim. Dunkin' asks for $250,000 in liquid assets and $500,000 net worth per shop. Royalty and advertising then take 8.5-11% of every sale.

roadmap.title: Cart: take the vendor course and get your license
roadmap.text: Every person who sells from a cart needs a Mobile Food Vending License: $53 for the food protection course for mobile vendors and $50 for the two-year license. Without it you cannot even join the waiting list for a cart permit.

roadmap.title: Cart: get on the waiting list for a supervisory license
roadmap.text: New year-round cart permits go only to holders of a supervisory license, handed out from a waiting list. The city adds 2,200 a year from July 2026 through 2031; advocates count more than 20,000 people waiting. A Restricted Area permit for private property has no waiting list.

roadmap.title: Cart: sign with a commissary and pass the cart inspection
roadmap.text: The cart must sleep in a Health Department-permitted commissary and return there daily for cleaning and supplies; you show the commissary agreement at the pre-permit inspection, in person, within six months of applying. Brewed coffee is the simplest cart class.

roadmap.title: Pop-up or market stand: get the temporary permit
roadmap.text: A Temporary Food Service Establishment permit costs $70 a year and covers events of 14 days or less, one event at a time. The organizer must give the Health Department the vendor list 30 days ahead. No permit: the stand is closed on the spot and fined $200-$2,000.

roadmap.title: Corner in someone else's shop: work under the host's permit
roadmap.text: A coffee counter inside a permitted restaurant or shop operates under the host's permit and the host's supervision, so the host carries the inspection risk and can end the arrangement. Put the rent, the hours and who owns the customers in writing.

ruleCards.title: Rent starts before sales do
ruleCards.text: NYC restaurant leases usually give 3-6 months of free rent. Renovating a former restaurant takes 3-5 months, an empty shell 6-9, and brokers count 8-12 months from signing to opening. Every month past the free period is rent with no income.

ruleCards.title: Good guy guaranty
ruleCards.text: New York's good guy guaranty ends your personal liability on the day you hand back the keys, if you gave written notice (usually 3-6 months), paid rent to that day and left the space broom-clean. Miss the notice and you can owe the rest of the lease.

ruleCards.title: How big the deposit gets
ruleCards.text: There is no legal cap on a commercial deposit. Brokers see 3-6 months of rent for tenants with credit and 6-12 months for startups and restaurants, often as a bank letter of credit that takes 2-3 weeks to issue and costs about 1-2% a year.

ruleCards.title: Rent goes up every year
ruleCards.text: Most NYC retail leases raise base rent by a fixed percentage each year, typically about 3%, compounding: $100 per square foot in year one is about $130 in year ten. Ask whether the increase is simple or compound before you sign.

ruleCards.title: You pay the landlord's tax increases
ruleCards.text: Most NYC store leases make the tenant pay a share of any rise in the building's property tax above a base year. If the base year is low, a reassessment lands on you: brokers see $10-$20 per square foot a year added in older buildings.

ruleCards.title: Staying past the lease
ruleCards.text: If you stay after the lease ends without a renewal, the holdover clause applies: typically 150% to 200% of the last rent, and New York courts enforce it. A commercial tenant has no legal right to renew.

ruleCards.title: Selling does not free you from the lease
ruleCards.text: When you sell and assign your lease, you stay liable for the rent unless the landlord releases you in writing, even if the landlord consented and takes rent from the buyer. Selling a majority of your LLC can count as an assignment too.

ruleCards.title: Who pays the broker
ruleCards.text: In New York City retail leasing the landlord normally pays one full brokerage commission, split between its broker and yours, so a tenant's broker costs you nothing directly. It is priced into the rent.

ruleCards.title: Free lease lawyer
ruleCards.text: The city's Commercial Lease Assistance Program reviews and negotiates leases for eligible small businesses at no charge and calls back within 3 business days. It served 812 businesses in the year to June 2025. It will not represent you in court.

ruleCards.title: Empty storefronts are leverage
ruleCards.text: About 11% of New York City storefronts were vacant in April 2026: 12.9% in Manhattan, 12.3% in Brooklyn, 9.5% in Queens, and 21% in the Financial District. A landlord with a store empty for a year will trade free rent for a signed lease.

ruleCards.title: Building without a permit
ruleCards.text: Construction without a Buildings permit costs 21 times the permit fee, at least $6,000 and up to $15,000 for a store, plus a Stop Work Order, and you still have to file the plans. Most cases start with a neighbor's 311 call.

ruleCards.title: Stop Work Order
ruleCards.text: Working against a Stop Work Order costs $6,000 the first time and $12,000 each time after. The Department of Buildings does not lift the order until the penalties are paid, and rent keeps running on the idle site.

ruleCards.title: Licensed plumber, licensed electrician
ruleCards.text: In New York City only a licensed master plumber may do plumbing and only a licensed electrician may wire. Unlicensed work is a misdemeanor with civil penalties from $2,500, cannot pass inspection, and gets torn out and redone.

ruleCards.title: What needs no permit
ruleCards.text: Painting, plastering, new cabinets, resurfacing floors and swapping a plumbing fixture need no Buildings permit. Moving a wall, a drain or a gas line does, with plans filed by a registered architect or engineer.

ruleCards.title: How long a Buildings permit takes
ruleCards.text: In 2025 the Department of Buildings finished a first plan review in 3.7 business days on average and took 20.3 days from application to approval; early in fiscal 2026 that rose to 23.6 days. Objections from the examiner restart the clock.

ruleCards.title: Asbestos report before any permit
ruleCards.text: For work in a building put up before April 1, 1987, the Buildings permit is not issued until a certified asbestos investigator files an ACP-5 report. Only buildings newer than that can claim the exemption.

ruleCards.title: Storefronts in historic districts
ruleCards.text: In a historic district every exterior change to a storefront needs a Landmarks permit first. Staff approve complete applications in 10-15 business days, and 95% of approvals never go to a hearing. The fee is $95 for the first $25,000 of work.

ruleCards.title: Waiting for gas
ruleCards.text: A State Senate survey of city restaurants found an average wait of 68 days for gas service; 69% waited at least 30 days and some up to a year. The utility connects only after the Buildings Department passes the piping.

ruleCards.title: Sales tax on your build-out
ruleCards.text: New York presumes work done for a tenant is temporary and taxable at 8.875%. If the lease makes the improvements the landlord's property, give the contractor a Certificate of Capital Improvement (Form ST-124) and the labor is tax-free.

ruleCards.title: A worker falls on your job
ruleCards.text: New York Labor Law §240 makes owners absolutely liable when a construction worker falls. Courts treat the tenant who hired the contractor as an owner. Before work starts, get insurance certificates that name you and the landlord.

ruleCards.title: Your contractor's unpaid bills
ruleCards.text: A subcontractor your contractor did not pay can file a mechanic's lien on the property for up to 8 months after its last work. Most leases make that your default. Clearing it takes a bond of 110% of the claim. Collect lien waivers with every payment.

ruleCards.title: Utility deposit
ruleCards.text: Con Edison may ask a new business for a security deposit of up to two times its average monthly bill, estimated from a similar business. You have the right to ask for the amount to be reviewed.

ruleCards.title: A free city project manager
ruleCards.text: Executive Order 18 of July 2026 tells Small Business Services to give each client of the NYC Business Express Service Team a project manager who identifies permits, helps apply and coordinates pre-opening inspections. The service is free.

ruleCards.title: Practice inspection for $100
ruleCards.text: A new restaurant that has begun serving food can buy one consultative inspection for $100 before its first graded visit. The inspector scores nothing and fines nothing, but a public health hazard must be fixed before they leave.

ruleCards.title: Permits do not come with the shop
ruleCards.text: Under NYC Health Code §5.11 a food permit is void the moment it is transferred to anyone not named on it. A buyer applies for a new one and may open on the 22nd day after applying. Liquor and sidewalk-cafe licenses do not transfer either.

ruleCards.title: Bulk sale notice
ruleCards.text: A buyer of business assets must file Form AU-196.10 with the Tax Department at least 10 days before paying or taking possession. Miss it and you personally owe the seller's unpaid sales tax, up to the purchase price or the assets' value.

ruleCards.title: Sales tax on a bought business
ruleCards.text: When you buy a shop you pay 8.875% sales tax on the furniture, fixtures and equipment part of the price, though not on inventory for resale, goodwill or the lease. How the contract splits the price decides the bill.

ruleCards.title: What a coffee shop sells for
ruleCards.text: US coffee shops and cafes sold between 2021 and 2025 went for a median 0.41 times yearly revenue and 2.0 times the owner's yearly earnings; the middle half fell between 1.5 and 2.55 times earnings. The median sale price in 2025 was $176,500.

ruleCards.title: Key money
ruleCards.text: Key money buys a lease and whatever is bolted to the room, not a customer base. It is worth paying only when the inherited rent is below market and enough years remain. New York listings range from $30,000 for a small cafe to $225,000 for a Village storefront.

ruleCards.title: You inherit the seller's unemployment record
ruleCards.text: When you buy all or part of a business in New York, the seller's unemployment-insurance experience account transfers to you and your rate is recalculated from the transfer date. Not reporting the purchase does not prevent it.

ruleCards.title: Borrowing to buy a business
ruleCards.text: An SBA 7(a) loan to start or buy a business requires at least 10% of the project cost from the buyer. A seller note can cover at most half of that, and only if the seller takes no payments for the whole loan term.

ruleCards.title: The 14-day rule for franchises
ruleCards.text: Federal rules require a franchisor to hand over its disclosure document at least 14 calendar days before you sign or pay anything. In New York the offering must also be registered with the Attorney General before it is sold.

ruleCards.title: What a coffee franchise takes
ruleCards.text: Gregorys Coffee charges a $35,000 fee, a 6% royalty and 2.5% for marketing on a $459,000-$946,000 investment. Dunkin' takes 5.9% plus 5% for advertising and expects $250,000 in liquid assets and $500,000 net worth per shop.

ruleCards.title: Vending without a license
ruleCards.text: Selling food from a cart with no license or no permit decal starts at $1,000 per summons in New York City, and a cart with no licensed vendor at it can be seized and forfeited.

ruleCards.title: Cart permits are capped
ruleCards.text: New year-round food cart permits go only to holders of a supervisory license from a waiting list. Local Laws 54 and 59 of 2026 add 2,200 a year from July 2026 through 2031. The first issue is free; renewal is $438 every two years.

ruleCards.title: A cart needs a commissary
ruleCards.text: Every food cart must be stored at a Health Department-permitted commissary and return there at least once a day for cleaning and supplies. No commissary agreement, no permit. Guides quote $300-$1,200 a month.

ruleCards.title: Pop-ups need a permit too
ruleCards.text: A stand at a street fair or market needs a $70 Temporary Food Service Establishment permit, good for events of 14 days or less, one event at a time. Without it the stand is closed on the spot and fined $200 to $2,000.

ruleCards.title: A kiosk in a park
ruleCards.text: A park kiosk or cart is a city concession won through a public request for proposals. The operator pays the higher of a guaranteed minimum yearly fee or a share of gross receipts: one 2024 agreement set $40,000 against 4% in year one.

monthlyCosts.name: Yearly rent increase written into the lease
monthlyCosts.note: A fixed yearly percentage increase is the most common escalation in NYC leases, typically about 3% (two broker sources); it compounds, so $100 per sq ft becomes about $130 in year ten. 3% x $6,000 = $180 a month from month 13, $365 from month 25. Zero in the first lease year.

monthlyCosts.name: Share of the building's property-tax increase (additional rent)
monthlyCosts.note: Law-firm guides: NYC store tenants usually pay their proportionate share of the building's real estate tax above a base year; a broker site says that on an older building with high taxes the pass-through can add $10-$20 per sq ft a year over time. Calculation for year one: tax attributable to an 800 sq ft store taken as $18 per sq ft a year ($14,400), growing 5% in the new city fiscal year = $720 a year = $60 a month. Both the $18 and the 5% are my assumptions; the real figure is in the lease and in the building's tax bill. City property-tax bills run on a July 1 fiscal year.

monthlyCosts.name: Bank fee for a letter of credit posted as the lease deposit
monthlyCosts.appliesIf: the deposit is posted as a standby letter of credit instead of cash
monthlyCosts.note: Lease guides put the yearly bank fee for a standby letter of credit at about 0.75-1.5% of its amount (others say 1-2%), plus an issuance fee; a new business must usually back it with cash, it is renewed every year and takes 2-3 weeks to issue (NYC broker sources). 1.5% x $18,000 = $270 a year = $23 a month. No bank rate sheet was seen.

monthlyCosts.name: Franchise royalty
monthlyCosts.note: Gregorys Coffee franchise site, seen in extract: royalty 6% of gross sales. Dunkin': 5.9% (several summaries of its disclosure document); Scooter's Coffee: 6% (2026 disclosure document summary). At the reference $51,000 a month this is $3,060.

monthlyCosts.name: Franchise marketing fund
monthlyCosts.note: Franchise directory summary of the Gregorys Coffee disclosure document: 2.5% of gross sales to the marketing fund on top of the royalty. Dunkin' charges 5% for advertising. At $51,000 a month: $1,275.

monthlyCosts.name: Commissary: overnight storage, cleaning, water and supplies for a cart
monthlyCosts.note: The rule is from the Health Department page (seen in extract): a cart must be stored at a permitted commissary and return at least once a day; the agreement is checked at the pre-permit inspection. The price is not official: a 2013/2018 Untapped Cities report gave $250-$300 a month for a garage space; 2026 vendor guides quote $300-$600 for basic access and $500-$1,500 for full service. $600 is my planning value between them.

monthlyCosts.name: Supervisory license renewal (cart)
monthlyCosts.note: Health Department guidance, seen in extract: the first supervisory license is issued without a fee; renewing it for two years costs $438 (veterans exempt). $438 / 24 = $18.25 a month. An older 2022 notice listed $230.

levers.name: Personal guaranty
levers.note: Legal mechanics are real (good guy guaranty: liability ends at surrender after written notice, typically 3-6 months; full guaranty: liability for the remaining term; deposits of 3-6 months with credit, 6-12 months for startups and restaurants). The mapping of deposit months to each option is a design value built from those ranges.

options.label: Good guy guaranty, 6-month notice, deposit of 4 months
Full personal guaranty, deposit of 3 months
No guaranty, deposit of 9 months

levers.name: Free rent for the build-out
levers.note: Real range: NYC restaurant leases typically give 3-6 months of free rent, up to 12 for heavy build-outs on a 10-year lease. The 4% rent premium for the longer concession and the permit-tied start are design values: landlords price free rent into the face rent, but no public rate exists.

options.label: Three months free, standard rent
Six months free, rent 4% higher for the whole term
Rent starts when the Buildings permit is issued, then three months free, rent 2% higher

levers.name: Checks before signing the lease
levers.note: The survey price is my estimate (an architect or engineer and an electrician for half a day each); no public fee was found. The game effect is real-world logic: every hidden attribute of the address (year built, landmark, Certificate of Occupancy, panel size, prior use, building arrears) is public record or visible on a walk-through.

options.label: Sign this week before someone else takes it
Records search and walk-through with an architect and an electrician ($2,500)

levers.name: Gas or all-electric
levers.note: Gas wait: NY State Senate survey of city restaurants (2017), average about 68 days, 69% at least 30 days, some up to a year. All-electric removes the gas track but can force a larger electrical service (see electrical_service_upgrade).

options.label: All-electric: espresso, ovens and water heater on electricity
Gas for the water heater and an oven

levers.name: Which contractor
levers.note: The price gap and the schedule effects are design values. The underlying facts are real: licensed trades are mandatory, a contractor's unpaid subcontractor can lien the property for 8 months, and the tenant who hires the crew can be liable under Labor Law 240 if a worker falls.

options.label: Contractor who builds cafes: insured, milestone payments, lien waivers
Lowest bid, 12% cheaper, half the money up front

levers.name: Build-out contingency
levers.note: Contractor guidance: 10-15% of hard costs (another contractor: 5-10%); a Spanish-language NYC guide advises 20%. Changes forced through with no reserve cost a 15-30% premium.

options.label: Keep 5% in reserve
Keep 15% in reserve
Keep 20% in reserve

levers.name: Construction pace
levers.note: After-hours variance fees are from the Buildings Department (seen in extract): filing fee $650 for 13-14 days plus $80 for each day of work. Two 14-day variances a month = 2 x (650 + 14 x 80) = $3,540; overtime premium on labor is my estimate ($2,200 a month: half of the labor on a $70,000 job, a quarter more hours at time and a half). The 25% shorter schedule is a design value.

options.label: Weekdays, regular hours
Evenings and weekends with an after-hours variance

levers.name: How you open
levers.note: The $100 consultative inspection is real (Health Code Chapter 21; only after food service has begun and before the first graded inspection). The size of the effect on inspection points is a design value.

options.label: Grand opening on day one
Two quiet weeks and a $100 consultative inspection

levers.name: Checks before buying a business
levers.note: Fee: New York guides put legal fees for a small business purchase at $1,800-$10,000 (another: $3,500-$25,000 for small and mid-sized sales); $6,000 covers the lawyer and an accountant matching register reports to bank deposits. What the review reveals is real: seller's sales-tax debt (bulk sale answer), liens on equipment, lease term left, true sales.

options.label: Trust the listing and the seller's word
Lawyer, accountant, lien search and bulk-sale notice ($6,000)

levers.name: When to apply for your own permits
levers.note: NYC Business: a new applicant may open on the 22nd day after submitting the application; Health Code §5.11 voids the seller's permit on transfer. Applying before closing costs nothing and removes the gap.

options.label: Apply 22 days before closing; the seller trades until the handover
Apply on closing day and stay shut until day 22

levers.name: First month after buying
levers.note: Design values. The research branch keeps 90% of regulars at a takeover; the split between a quiet handover and an immediate rebrand is mine. Seller training of 2-4 weeks is usual in business sales but no figure was sourced.

options.label: Keep the staff, the menu and the name for now
New name, new menu, new team from day one

levers.name: Where the cart stands
levers.note: Rule from NYC Business and Health Code Article 89 (seen in extract): a Restricted Area permit lets a cart vend on private, commercially zoned property or Parks land under a written agreement with the owner; it has no waiting list and no cap, but the sidewalk in front of the building is public space and not covered. The $1,500 site rent is a design value: no public figure exists.

options.label: Public sidewalk (needs a capped citywide permit)
Private plaza or lot under a written agreement (no waiting list)

events.name: Buildings permits slow down
events.text: The Department of Buildings is taking longer to approve plans this season. Anyone still waiting for a permit waits a few days more.
events.note: NYS Comptroller audit release (July 2026), seen in extract: application-to-approval averaged 20.3 days in 2025 and rose to 23.6 days in the first four months of fiscal 2026: 23.6 / 20.3 = 1.16. New field permitWaitDays: needs engine support.

events.name: Construction costs up 7%
events.text: Contractors in New York are quoting more than last year. A build-out not yet under contract costs more.
events.note: Cushman & Wakefield 2026 Retail Fit-Out Cost Guide, seen in extract: New York City in-line retail fit-outs rose 7.0% year over year to $181 per sq ft (national average $157, up 1.4%). That figure is plain retail, not food service. New field buildoutCost: applies to contracts signed while the event is active.

events.name: Tariff on European espresso machines
events.text: Italian machines and grinders carry a 15% import tariff. Dealers pass it on to new orders.
events.note: Trade press, seen in extract: since late July 2025 the United States applies a 15% tariff to goods from the European Union, appliances included. Full pass-through to the price of imported espresso machines and grinders is my assumption (upper bound); some dealers absorbed part of it. New field equipmentCost: applies to imported setup items bought while active.

events.name: One storefront in nine is empty
events.text: Landlords with empty stores are giving more free rent to sign a tenant. Leases signed now start cheaper.
events.note: NYC Comptroller, seen in extract: citywide storefront vacancy 11.0% on April 15, 2026 (Manhattan 12.9%, Brooklyn 12.3%, Queens 9.5%, Financial District 21.1%). The effect is a design value: one extra free month on a three-month concession (x1.33) in districts above the city average. New field freeRentMonths.

suppliers.what: Listings of operating coffee shops and built-out spaces offered for key money, with asking price, stated sales and cash flow
suppliers.whereToFind: BizBuySell and BizQuest (filter New York, coffee shops and cafes); restaurant brokers; signs in windows; ask your roaster who is selling
suppliers.note: Asking prices seen in November 2026 extracts: Sunnyside cafe $385,000 with $150,000 stated cash flow; 40-year-old Queens coffee shop $235,000 / $145,000; 558 sq ft Brooklyn cafe $125,000 / $71,157 with seller financing; a cafe at $120,000 / $40,126. Asking prices, not closed sales.

suppliers.what: Commercial lease review and negotiation; asset purchase agreement, bulk-sale notice and escrow when buying a shop
suppliers.whereToFind: Free: NYC Commercial Lease Assistance Program (888-SBS-4NYC). Paid: restaurant and hospitality law firms; ask for a flat fee and what it covers
suppliers.examples: NYC Small Business Services legal providers
suppliers.note: New York guides: legal fees for a small business purchase about $1,800-$10,000; one firm publishes 0.85% of the deal with a $1,800 minimum. The pack budgets $3,500 for a lease lawyer.

suppliers.what: Filing representative for Department of Buildings and Landmarks applications; certified asbestos investigator for the ACP-5 report
suppliers.whereToFind: Your architect brings both; the Department of Environmental Protection lists certified asbestos investigators; ask other shop owners on the block
suppliers.examples: Registered filing representatives; DEP-certified asbestos investigators
suppliers.note: Only a certified asbestos investigator may file an ACP-5; survey prices of $400-$1,500 are from secondary guides.

suppliers.what: A project manager who maps your permits and coordinates pre-opening inspections; free lease review; free energy survey with equipment incentives
suppliers.whereToFind: NYC Business Express Service Team (NYC BEST) through Small Business Services; Con Edison small business program
suppliers.examples: NYC BEST, Commercial Lease Assistance Program, Con Edison Small Business Direct Install
suppliers.note: Executive Order 18 (July 20, 2026) orders a dedicated project manager for each NYC BEST client. Con Edison's 2026 small-business factsheet says incentives may cover up to 100% of eligible cost for lighting, refrigeration and HVAC upgrades.

suppliers.what: A brand, a design and a supply chain in exchange for a fee, a royalty and control over your build-out
suppliers.whereToFind: The franchisor's own franchise site; the disclosure document; franchisees listed in Item 20
suppliers.note: Total initial investment from disclosure-document summaries: Gregorys Coffee $459,150-$946,000; Dunkin' $443,000-$1,832,500; Caffe Aronne $98,000-$268,000 (aggregator figures). Starbucks does not franchise.

suppliers.what: A cart built to Health Department rules and a permitted commissary to store, clean and supply it
suppliers.whereToFind: Cart makers in Queens and Brooklyn; the Health Department's list of permitted commissaries; other vendors at the commissary gate
suppliers.note: Cart price points seen: hot dog cart from $5,790; a full-service stainless coffee cart listed at $16,500. Commissary prices are not published.

suppliers.what: A stall at a seasonal food market, or a city concession for a kiosk or cart in a park
suppliers.whereToFind: Market operators' vendor applications; NYC Parks concession opportunities and the City Record for requests for proposals
suppliers.examples: Smorgasburg (Williamsburg, Prospect Park, World Trade Center); Battery kiosks
suppliers.note: Parks concessions pay the greater of a guaranteed minimum yearly fee or a percentage of gross receipts (one 2024 agreement: $40,000 against 4% in year one). Market stall fees were not found in this session.
